Bohr Model. It is a simplified atomic model proposed by Niels Bohr in nineteen thirteen, depicting electrons orbiting the nucleus in discrete, quantized shells or energy levels rather than a diffuse electron cloud. Though superseded by quantum mechanics and the Schrödinger equation, the Bohr model successfully explained the hydrogen spectrum and introduced the revolutionary idea of energy quantization. It remains pedagogically valuable for understanding atomic structure and the origin of spectral lines.

The model assumes electrons orbit the nucleus like planets around the sun, but only in specific allowed orbits corresponding to discrete energy levels. This quantization was revolutionary. The first Bohr radius, approximately zero point fifty-three Ångströms, defines the size of the hydrogen atom. Successive orbitals are at distances proportional to n squared, where n equals one, two, three, and so on.

The energy of the n-th orbit in hydrogen is negative thirteen point six electron-volts divided by n squared. Electrons can only occupy these discrete levels, not the spaces between. Spectral lines arise when electrons transition between energy levels. They absorb photons to jump to higher levels—excitation—or emit photons when falling to lower levels—de-excitation. The Rydberg formula, which relates frequency to orbital transitions, predicted the frequency of emitted light with remarkable accuracy for hydrogen.

Angular momentum is quantized in the Bohr model. It equals n times the reduced Planck constant, explaining why only certain orbits are allowed. The model fails for multi-electron atoms because it does not account for electron-electron repulsion and relativistic effects, and it incorrectly predicts orbital shapes. The Schrödinger equation and quantum mechanics replaced the Bohr model with orbitals—probability distributions—rather than definite trajectories. The principal quantum number n remains quantized but the path is undefined. These connections link the model to atoms themselves, to electrons as the orbiting particles, to quantum mechanics as the fuller theory, to Niels Bohr as the developer, and to spectroscopy as the observational technique that validates the predictions.
